newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking French truckers block ports, German border.
newsitem.headline: Striking French truckers block ports, German border.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers blocked Channel ports and German border crossings on Monday as they stepped up protests on the eighth day of the most serious labour unrest in France this year.

Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe renewed an appeal to truckers and haulage companies to reach a deal in talks over the strike slowly squeezing the French economy and provoking frictions with France's neighbours.

"I'm following the talks hour by hour," Juppe said after a marathon all-night round of talks between bosses and drivers ended in deadlock over strikers' demands for higher wages, shorter hours and retirement at age 55 rather than 60.

"The government has done everything to get these talks under way. They must now resume and finish," he said. After their abortive 14-hour session, unions and bosses were to meet for a new round in Paris on Monday hosted by mediator Robert Cros.
The dispute is the most serious unrest since a 24-day round of public sector strikes against the centre-right government almost paralysed the country in late 1995.
The Communist-led CGT union called on union members to rally around the truckers' barriers in a national show of solidarity on Wednesday.
Five rail unions also called on their members to support the strikes "in a way they will judge necessary".

The truckers, buoyed by an opinion poll showing broad public support, hardened their protests, tightening blocades of refineries and oil depots, blocking the Channel ports of Calais and Boulogne and frontier crossings with Germany in Alsace.
They let cars and buses embark on Channel ferries. A port spokesman in Calais said British truck drivers briefly joined the action in sympathy for about an hour, disrupting ferry loadings for cars.
French truckers stopped trucks at the German border in Strasbourg, Gambsheim, Beinheim, Lauterbourg and Wissembourg.

The actions added to the woes of cross-Channel travellers, already hit by the closure of the Channel Tunnel to all but freight trains after a fire last week. Some drivers wanting to cross to Britain drove to Belgian ports.
The state road information centre said there were 136 truckers' barricades on major routes in France on Monday afternoon, up from 62 on Sunday night, with tens of thousands of trucks involved.

Truckers targeted oil refineries and fuel depots, blocking industrial zones in Le Havre and Rouen in the north-west, and cutting off the last petrol depot still accessible in the Pyrenees-Atlantiques region, at Boucau near Bayonne.

"The majority of refineries are blocked or have an uncertain situation," a spokeswoman for the oil industry association UFIP said. Only four of 13 were unaffected. About 100 of the country's 18,000 petrol stations had run out of fuel.
Carmaker Renault SA said it halted work at its Douai plant in northern France because of a lack of supplies.
The protests also crept closer to Paris.

Protesters blocked Elf Aquitaine's Grandpuits refinery near the capital and access roads to a major wholesale food market. The main motorway north of the capital was briefly cut to one lane on the southbound carriage near Roissy airport.

The British government urged a quick end to the strike. German and Spanish officials expressed sympathy with the French government's efforts to end the disruption, which has trapped throusands of foreign trucks.
An IPSOS opinion poll for France-2 television showed an overwhelming 74 percent of French people sympathised with the strikers and 87 percent found their demands "fairly justified".
